questions.text: A coastal residential site in Batangas is exposed to salt spray and experiences seasonal flooding. Which of the following plant selections would be most appropriate for this environment?

options.text: Japanese cherry trees, imported ornamental shrubs, and exotic groundcovers, which are not typically suited for saline conditions or flooding
Narra trees, fire tree (Delonix regia), pili, and native salt-tolerant groundcovers
Mango, calamansi, and temperate-zone vegetables, which may not thrive in high salinity or waterlogged soils
Bamboo only; monoculture reduces maintenance but may not provide the necessary ecological diversity

rationale.a: Japanese cherry trees do not thrive in coastal salt spray; exotic species require more maintenance and may fail.
rationale.c: Mango and calamansi can work, but vegetables are temporary and not suitable for long-term landscaping structure.
rationale.d: Monoculture creates pest vulnerability and biodiversity loss; diversity is essential.
rationale.correct: Narra is a native, salt-tolerant Philippine tree. Fire tree thrives in tropical conditions. Pili is native and produces crops. Native salt-tolerant groundcovers (such as Philippine sedge or vetiver) survive coastal exposure. These species reduce irrigation needs, resist local pests, and provide ecological value.
rationale.takeaway: Select native species adapted to local climate, soil, and hazards (salt spray, flooding). Native plants thrive with minimal input, reducing lifecycle costs and environmental impact.

questions.text: A coastal site requires stabilization of a 20m slope subject to monsoon rainfall. Which landscape and engineering approach would best prevent erosion while maintaining ecological value?

options.text: Concrete retaining wall; bare concrete requires no maintenance and provides maximum stability, though it lacks ecological benefits
Deep-rooted native shrubs (santan, tilapia), vetiver grass strips, and bioengineered slope drains to stabilize soil and reduce runoff velocity
Remove all vegetation and construct a gabion wall for rapid installation, prioritizing structural integrity over ecological considerations
Install imported groundcover requiring year-round irrigation; ensure aesthetic appearance but with high maintenance needs

rationale.a: Concrete walls fail if not properly drained; can become focal points for erosion at base. Ecologically sterile.
rationale.c: Gabion walls are temporary; vegetation-integrated solutions are superior for monsoon-prone sites.
rationale.d: Imported species with irrigation requirements increase lifecycle costs and fail under monsoon stress.
rationale.correct: Native deep-rooted plants (shrubs, grasses) stabilize soil through root networks, slow rainfall infiltration, and reduce runoff velocity. Vetiver grass is particularly effective for erosion control in tropical regions. Bioengineered drains channel water safely. This approach provides long-term stability, reduces maintenance costs, supports habitat, and integrates with the tropical landscape.
rationale.takeaway: Slope stabilization in tropical regions benefits from bioengineering: native plants, soil amendments, and drainage. Vegetation is not supplementary—it is the primary stabilizing agent.

questions.code_citation: Soil & Water Conservation Standards; Bioengineering Best Practices; DENR Guidelines

questions.text: A 3,000 m² neighborhood plaza is designed with permeable paving to infiltrate stormwater. The plaza slopes at 2%, and the underlying soil has a moderate infiltration rate of 10mm/hour. For a 50mm rainfall event, what infiltration challenge should the designer address?

options.text: No challenge; 2% slope and 10mm/hour infiltration rate easily handle 50mm rainfall, assuming no additional runoff from adjacent areas
The 50mm rainfall will fall faster than the soil can infiltrate (10mm/hour); additional measures (overflow drain, bioretention, or raised paving) are necessary
Permeable paving alone is insufficient; eliminate the plaza design and consider alternative stormwater management strategies
Increase slope to 5% to accelerate drainage, ensuring rapid removal of surface water during peak rainfall events

rationale.a: Infiltration rate is dramatically lower than rainfall intensity; ponding is inevitable without mitigation.
rationale.c: Permeable paving is valuable; supplementary drainage (not elimination) is the solution.
rationale.d: Slope steepness does not increase infiltration rate; it only accelerates flow off-site.
rationale.correct: A 50mm rainfall event typically occurs over 1–2 hours in monsoon conditions, delivering rainfall at ~25–50mm/hour. The soil infiltration rate of 10mm/hour is far slower than rainfall intensity, causing surface ponding. Designer must incorporate overflow drains, bioretention basins, or raised pavement sections to prevent standing water and structural damage.
rationale.takeaway: Compare infiltration rate (mm/hour) to rainfall intensity (mm/hour). When rainfall intensity > infiltration rate, design overflow management: bioretention, underdrains, or surface drainage paths.

questions.text: A subdivision landscape must balance three competing constraints: 30% open space requirement (PD 957), 40% hardscape for parking/roads, and 30% greenscape for livability. On a 50,000 m² site, how should land be allocated, and what compromise resolves the apparent conflict?

options.text: 30% open space (15,000) + 40% hardscape (20,000) = 35,000 m²; only 15,000 m² for greenscape (30% unachievable), leading to a shortfall in greenscape allocation
30% open space must include integrated hardscape and greenscape; allocate 15% hardscape, 15% greenscape within the 30% open space total
Hardscape and greenscape are separate; prioritize hardscape (parking/roads) first; greenscape on remainder, which may not meet the full 30% requirement
The constraints are incompatible; choose the highest priority (usually hardscape for vehicular access), potentially sacrificing greenscape

rationale.a: Correctly identifies the apparent conflict but does not resolve it.
rationale.c: Separates hardscape and greenscape; misses the integration insight.
rationale.d: Assumes conflict is irresolvable; design integration solves it.
rationale.correct: The resolution is integration: 30% open space (PD 1216) includes roads/sidewalks/community facilities; non-buildable parks/recreation (3.5-9%) is softscape. Parking typically outside open space reservation. (turf, trees, gardens: 15%). This configuration achieves all three goals: (1) 30% public/common area per PD 957, (2) sufficient hardscape for circulation/parking, (3) meaningful greenscape (15%) for cooling, ecology, and livability. Misunderstanding this integration creates false conflicts.
rationale.takeaway: Open space (PD 957) is a container that includes both hardscape and softscape. Strategic allocation within the 30% envelope balances circulation, parking, and greenscape to maximize livability without violating code requirements.

questions.text: A bioretention basin is designed to capture stormwater from a 40m × 25m catchment area. The catchment slopes at 4%, and the basin dimensions are 10m × 6m × 0.8m deep (length × width × depth). Estimate the maximum volume the basin can absorb and assess whether it adequately handles typical monsoon runoff.

options.text: Basin capacity 48 m³; adequate for most events, assuming average rainfall intensity
Basin capacity 48 m³; likely inadequate for intense monsoon rainfall
Basin capacity 100 m³; adequate for all events, including extreme weather conditions
Basin capacity 240 m³; exceeds typical requirements, providing a significant safety margin

rationale.a: While volume is correct, monsoon rainfall intensity exceeds capacity.
rationale.c: Basin dimensions do not support 100 m³ capacity at 0.8m depth.
rationale.d: Calculation error; basin volume is 48 m³, not 240 m³.
rationale.correct: Basin volume = 10 × 6 × 0.8 = 48 m³. For a 1,000 m² catchment area, a 50mm rainfall event produces 50 m³ of runoff. A 100mm event (common in Philippine monsoons) produces 100 m³—far exceeding the 48 m³ basin capacity. Thus, the basin is undersized for typical monsoon intensity. Additional drainage (perforated underdrain, overflow spillway) is necessary.
rationale.takeaway: Size bioretention basins based on design storm (typically 25mm or 50mm depending on local standards, up to 100mm for high-risk areas). Philippine monsoon regions require larger basins or multiple features. Calculate: Runoff (mm) × Catchment Area (m²) ÷ 1,000 = Runoff Volume (m³).

questions.code_citation: EPA Stormwater Best Practices; Bioretention Design

questions.text: A subdivision master plan allocates 30% open space (per PD 957) but the landscape consultant notes that the open space is fragmented into small, isolated patches rather than one contiguous area. What is the primary concern with this fragmentation, and what recommendation should be made?

options.text: Fragmentation is acceptable if total area meets the 30% requirement; no change needed, although this overlooks usability issues.
Fragmentation reduces usability and accessibility; consolidate open space into larger, programmable zones connected by continuous pathways
Fragmentation increases green space benefits through distributed cooling; maintain current design, which may not address usability.
Fragmentation is economical; no recommendation needed, but this ignores potential accessibility problems.

rationale.a: Area alone does not satisfy the spirit of open space requirements; usability is critical.
rationale.c: While distributed cooling has merit, larger contiguous spaces provide greater ecological and social benefit.
rationale.d: Fragmented maintenance is often more expensive and results in neglect.
rationale.correct: While PD 957/PD 1216 specify 30% area (with density-based allocation), landscape standards recommend consolidated, usable open space for functionality, though not legally mandated. Fragmented patches cannot support community activities (gatherings, sports, recreation), are difficult to maintain, and isolate residents. Consolidating into fewer, larger zones with accessible connections ensures functionality and social equity.
rationale.takeaway: Open space requirements are not merely quantitative (30%); they are qualitative (usable, accessible, programmed). Larger contiguous zones connected by pathways serve communities far better than scattered fragments.

questions.text: A residential subdivision covers 80,000 m². AcAccording to PD 1216 amending PD 957 Sec 31, subdivisions ≥1ha reserve 30% gross for open space (including roads), but non-buildable parks/recreation is 3.5%-9% by density. Without density specified, state actual requirement depends on density (e.g., low-density: 3.5% = 2,800 m²).pliant?

options.text: 24,000 m² required; 20,000 m² is non-compliant
24,000 m² required; 20,000 m² is compliant
30,000 m² required; 20,000 m² is non-compliant
20,000 m² required; 20,000 m² is compliant

rationale.b: While the calculation of 24,000 m² is correct, 20,000 m² does not meet the requirement.
rationale.c: 30,000 m² would represent 37.5%, exceeding the requirement.
rationale.d: 20,000 m² is only 25%, less than the 30% mandate.
rationale.correct: PD 957 mandates 30% of gross area as open space. 80,000 × 0.30 = 24,000 m² required. The proposed 20,000 m² falls short by 4,000 m², making it non-compliant.
rationale.takeaway: PD 957 open space requirement = Gross Area × 30%. Always apply to gross area, not net buildable area. Non-compliant projects cannot proceed without redesign.

questions.text: A neighborhood park of 5,000 m² is designed with the following allocation: 60% paving (plazas, pathways), 30% turf and softscape, 10% structures (pavilions, restrooms). Is this hardscape-softscape balance appropriate for a residential neighborhood, and what adjustment would you recommend?

options.text: Yes, appropriate; paving dominates for durability and accessibility, which are key considerations in urban park design
No; recommend reducing paving to 40% and increasing softscape to 50% for shade, cooling, and quality
Yes, appropriate; 60% paving is standard for all park types, ensuring uniformity across different environments
No; recommend all softscape; paving is unnecessary, as natural surfaces provide better environmental benefits

rationale.a: While paving provides durability, excessive hardscape in residential areas reduces quality of life.
rationale.c: Park type matters; residential, commercial, and industrial parks require different balances.
rationale.d: Some hardscape is essential for accessibility (BP 344) and circulation; elimination is impractical.
rationale.correct: For residential neighborhoods, shade trees and cooling are essential for livability. A 60% hardscape is excessive and creates heat island effect, dust, and poor microclimate. Rebalancing to 40% paving (accessible but efficient), 50% softscape (trees, shrubs, turf for shade and cooling), and 10% structures better serves community needs and resilience. This aligns with landscape architecture best practices.
rationale.takeaway: Hardscape-softscape ratio varies by site type. Residential/community parks: aim for 40–50% hardscape, 40–50% softscape. Industrial/logistics: higher hardscape. Always balance function (access, drainage) with livability (shade, cooling, beauty).

questions.text: An architect is designing outdoor spaces for a 15,000 m² residential community. The design must include accessible pathways, gathering areas, activity zones, and buffer zones. Which spatial organization approach best balances functionality and walkability?

options.text: Concentrate all gathering spaces near the entrance; minimize internal pathways to reduce construction costs and simplify maintenance.
Organize outdoor rooms (gathering, activity, buffer, circulation) distributed throughout with continuous accessible pathways connecting all zones
Separate active and passive zones with no direct connections; use multiple entrances to facilitate diverse access points and reduce congestion.
Design one large plaza; eliminate redundant pathways to maximize open space and minimize landscape maintenance.

rationale.a: Concentrating spaces at the entrance excludes interior residents; poor equity.
rationale.c: Separation without connections reduces walkability and accessibility.
rationale.d: One large plaza overwhelms small groups; redundant pathways are not a liability—they offer choice and safety.
rationale.correct: Outdoor rooms distributed throughout the site with accessible pathways (per BP 344) create multiple social nodes, reduce crowding, and ensure all residents can safely access community spaces. This design maximizes usability, equity, and livability.
rationale.takeaway: Landscape design for residential communities should distribute gathering and activity spaces throughout, connected by continuous accessible pathways. Multiple entry/exit points and rest areas support elderly and mobility-limited residents.

questions.code_citation: BP 344 (Accessibility Law); Landscape Planning Best Practices

questions.text: A landscape design incorporates 2,000 m² of turf, 800 m² of tree canopy (estimated), and 500 m² of shrub masses in a 5,000 m² site. What is the approximate greenscape percentage, and does this meet residential community livability standards?

options.text: Greenscape = 54% (3,300 m² ÷ 5,000); exceeds typical 30–40% target
Greenscape = 20% (1,000 m² ÷ 5,000); insufficient for livability
Greenscape = 40% (2,000 m² ÷ 5,000); adequate but conservative
Cannot determine without knowing rainfall and irrigation water

rationale.b: Under-calculates greenscape; fails to include trees and shrubs (only counts turf).
rationale.c: Under-counts greenscape; only counts turf (2,000 m²), ignoring 800 m² canopy + 500 m² shrubs.
rationale.d: Greenscape percentage is independent of rainfall; usability and area calculation are the metrics.
rationale.correct: Greenscape includes turf (2,000) + tree canopy (800) + shrubs (500) = 3,300 m². Percentage = 3,300 ÷ 5,000 = 66%. This far exceeds the residential community standard of 30–40% greenscape, ensuring excellent shade, cooling, microclimate quality, and resident satisfaction. Over-provision of greenscape is an asset, not a liability.
rationale.takeaway: Greenscape calculation: sum all soft landscape elements (turf + tree canopy + shrub masses). High greenscape percentage (>50%) provides superior cooling, reduced heat island effect, improved habitat, and better livability. Target 40–60% for residential sites.

questions.code_citation: Landscape Planning Standards; Residential Livability Guidelines
